medical.title: How conversations shape decisions about dementia care
medical.summary: When someone is living with dementia, decisions about their care can have a significant impact on their health and quality of life. But how are these decisions made, particularly when family members or friends are also involved?

medical.title: Cannabis addiction in pregnancy linked to higher risk of postpartum psychiatric crises
medical.summary: Women diagnosed with cannabis use disorder during pregnancy were more likely to end up in an emergency room for a psychiatric problem in the year after giving birth, according to a study of more than 2 million California deliveries.

medical.title: Going to the park at least once a week can improve children's mental health
medical.summary: Children who visit parks and playgrounds at least once a week may have better mental health and social development as they grow up. That's according to a new study by the University of Exeter, published in Epidemiology and Community Health. The paper is titled "Park Visits and Social-Emotional Development throughout Childhood: A Longitudinal Analysis of ALSPAC."

medical.title: Successful sleep apnea treatment may lead to unexpected weight gain
medical.summary: A new study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) and Soroka University Medical Center may have uncovered a biological mechanism behind why many adults and children gain weight following successful treatment for obstructive sleep apnea. The research, conducted on mice and published in Scientific Reports, suggests that the body retains a persistent "metabolic memory" that continues to drive increased appetite even after normal breathing is restored.

medical.title: Study identifies antidepressants that get patients well and keep them well
medical.summary: Worldwide, nearly 6% of people experience depression. Many of them continue taking antidepressants after achieving symptomatic improvement, among other reasons to prevent a relapse of depression. An international team of researchers investigated which antidepressants, if any, can not only get patients well but also keep them well (sustained response).

medical.title: Deaf patients get a raw deal in NHS hospitals, illustrative case history suggests
medical.summary: Deaf patients get a raw deal in NHS hospitals, suggests an illustrative case history of a deaf person's experience as an inpatient, published in the online journal BMJ Case Reports. During his hospital stay, reasonable adjustments to facilitate access to services—a key tenet of U.K. disability legislation—weren't made; the need for a professional British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter wasn't recognized soon enough; and frontline staff weren't adequately trained in how to support him.

medical.title: Government guidance indicates 95% of processed foods are unhealthy
medical.summary: More than 95% of processed or ultra-processed food products would be classified as unhealthy under UK government dietary guidance, according to new UCL-led research. The study, published in BMJ Medicine, found that the official public health definitions used to identify and regulate food and drink products in the U.K. varied widely in what proportion of processed and ultraprocessed products they classed as unhealthy, while systems such as traffic light labels failed to identify more than half of these unhealthy packaged foods.

medical.title: Three-layer model maps how protein-modifying enzymes may help regulate immunity
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Tsukuba have proposed a "three-tiered proteostasis model" for describing immune regulation by protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs), comprising protein arginine methylation, free methylarginine generation from protein turnover and methyltransferase-independent interactions with RNA and proteins. The framework integrates emerging evidence linking PRMTs to immune regulation, metabolism, vascular function and age-associated inflammation.

medical.title: Why does cancer rarely spread to the heart? Researchers develop organ-on-a-chip platform to find out
medical.summary: Researchers from the University of Toronto have created a new multi-organ-on-a-chip device to investigate why the heart is one of the least common sites of cancer metastasis, creating new opportunities for cancer research and drug discovery.

medical.title: Digitally supported care model improves serum urate target attainment in gout
medical.summary: For patients with gout, a physician-supervised treat-to-target (T2T) care model improves serum urate (SUA) target attainment, according to a study published online Nov. 4 in Arthritis & Rheumatology.

medical.title: New biomarker may extend detection window for date-rape drug GHB
medical.summary: Every hour is critical when it comes to detecting the use of drugs used to render victims unconscious. The substance GHB, which is commonly used in this way, is excreted rapidly from blood and urine. Researchers at the University of Zurich have been evaluating a new biomarker using urine samples from real forensic cases. This biomarker can indicate earlier GHB intake even when the drug is no longer detectable using conventional analysis.

medical.title: Lung ultrasound predicts progression of interstitial lung abnormalities in rheumatoid arthritis
medical.summary: Lung ultrasound (LUS) can predict radiologic progression of interstitial lung abnormalities (ILAs) in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), according to a study published in the November issue of Arthritis & Rheumatology.

medical.title: About half have meaningful drop in long COVID symptoms by 36 months, study finds
medical.summary: About one-half of persons with likely long COVID (LC) after first severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection experience a meaningful reduction in symptoms by 36 months, according to a study published online Nov. 3 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

medical.title: Prostate cancer drug combination adds toxicity without clear benefit for tumors lacking targetable mutations
medical.summary: The prospective, multicenter, randomized phase 2 ZZ-FIRST clinical trial, led by the Vall d'Hebron Institute of Oncology's (VHIO) Prostate Cancer Group, evaluated the androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) enzalutamide plus the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) talazoparib versus enzalutamide alone in patients with high-tumor-burden metastatic prostate cancer who had not previously received hormone therapy.

science.title: Mental health app may help unemployed people find jobs, six-week trial suggests
science.summary: Losing a job can be a life-shattering experience. And when depression complicates a job search, unemployment can become a vicious cycle. Now, a Northwestern University–led clinical trial suggests a new intervention may break that cycle: a phone app, named DRIVEN, that combines weekly self-guided mental health exercises (to reduce stress and increase motivation) with job-seeking strategies.

science.title: A new tool makes biodiversity conservation planning more efficient and reproducible
science.summary: ZonationR is a new tool that simplifies the use of Zonation to identify priority areas for biodiversity conservation. It brings all stages of the conservation planning analysis together in one automated and reproducible workflow and helps users systematically explore and compare alternative conservation scenarios.

science.title: Genetic ancestry plays a key role in the migration of Cory's shearwaters
science.summary: To what extent do genes influence the migratory routes of birds? The factors that determine the long-distance migrations of seabirds are not yet fully understood. Now, a study published in the journal Molecular Ecology reveals that, in the case of Cory's shearwater, an individual's genetic ancestry is a more significant factor in their migratory decisions than their social environment in the breeding colony.

science.title: Earliest known compact quasar pair poses a black hole growth puzzle
science.summary: The oldest pair of compact quasars ever observed has been found only 900 million years after the Big Bang. Scientists say there is no theoretical explanation for how the pair of actively feeding black holes grew so massive at such an early time in the history of the universe. The pair of quasars has been given the Hawaiian nickname Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

science.title: New organic iron-sulfur framework boosts photosynthesis and carbon fixation
science.summary: Iron-sulfur clusters are ancient protein cofactors that are essential for electron transport, enzyme catalysis and photosynthesis. However, their sensitivity to oxygen and inherent instability have long hindered their practical application.

science.title: How ripples in space-time can reveal new exoplanets
science.summary: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets—worlds beyond our solar system—throughout our galaxy.

science.title: European eels transmit a herpesvirus through bites, revealing another route for fish infections
science.summary: Contrary to what was previously believed, viruses infecting fish are not transmitted exclusively through water acting as an abiotic vector. A team of researchers from the University of Liège has demonstrated that a virus affecting European eels can spread very efficiently through biting during aggressive interactions between individuals.

science.title: Where AI can aid chemistry research and where reliability falls short
science.summary: Researchers from the Skoltech AI Center, together with colleagues from the Zelinsky Institute of Organic Chemistry of the Russian Academy of Sciences, ITMO University and other institutions, have published a paper in Chemical Society Reviews that examines where AI produces measurable value in a chemical research workflow, how to assess its reliability and why a strong benchmark result does not necessarily translate into laboratory performance.

science.title: Repurposing the internet's backbone to advance whale monitoring
science.summary: Bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut, at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics, has spent the past several years eavesdropping on the conversations of whales. But instead of using underwater microphones like other marine scientists, she listens by tapping into fiber-optic cables lying on the ocean floor—a powerful tool to aid in marine mammal conservation.

science.title: Rerouting ships to avoid killing whale sharks has little cost, study finds
science.summary: Redirecting shipping traffic to avoid collisions with whale sharks has very little impact on fuel use, according to new research led by the University of Southampton published in Royal Society Open Science.

science.title: Ancient rocks reveal when Earth's tectonic engine 'switched on'
science.summary: Scientists have identified a major turning point in Earth's geological history, when the processes shaping the planet's crust changed dramatically and began to resemble the plate tectonics we see today—about 2.5 billion years ago.

science.title: High-achieving disadvantaged students are far less likely to take and pass entrance exams for selective schools
science.summary: Disadvantaged students are less likely than their more advantaged peers with similar attainment to take and pass entrance exams for selective schools, and introducing an opt-out system for the tests would only deliver a small boost.

science.title: Scientists anchor first scientific animal name to a modern-day spider
science.summary: Scientists led by the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History have restored the physical reference of one of the most historically significant names in biology. In a paper published in Taxonomy, researchers designated a new type specimen, or neotype, for Araneus angulatus, the first animal species described using binomial nomenclature, the two-part naming system that scientists use today to identify and classify living organisms. The designation reconnects the name to a physical specimen decades after the original name-bearing spiders disappeared.

science.title: Gamma radiation transforms brittle bioplastic into 'superstructure' hydrogel
science.summary: Biomaterials engineers have created a "superstructure" hydrogel that could be an eco-friendly tool used in medical technologies and as a recovery aid for surgical procedures. The research is published in the journal Macromolecular Rapid Communications.

science.title: The psychology of saving electricity: How comparisons can curb consumption
science.summary: Simple psychological interventions are often enough to encourage people to change their behavior—and this is also true when it comes to saving electricity. A new study by Mannheim-based consumer psychologist Dr. Yavor Paunov and colleagues shows that comparing one's own electricity consumption with that of others as well as practical energy-saving tips can help reduce energy consumption.

science.title: Microscopy upgrade sharpens images fivefold without sacrificing tissue imaging depth
science.summary: Researchers at Texas A&M University have cracked a problem that has limited biological imaging for years: seeing fine cellular detail while looking deep inside living tissue. The new microscopy technique resolves structures smaller than 100 nanometers, roughly a thousand times thinner than a human hair, without giving up the ability to image deep into intact samples.

science.title: Water molecules turn out to be secret messengers for magnetism
science.summary: Water is not usually thought of as a magnetic material. But a new study led by researchers at Tohoku University's Institute of Multidisciplinary Research for Advanced Materials, in collaboration with National Taipei University of Technology (Taipei Tech), has found that tiny shifts in the orientation of water molecules can flip on magnetic partnerships between metal ions that are not even directly bonded to each other.

science.title: Harnessing laser nuisance achieves record resolution for atomic measurements
science.summary: A shoebox-sized color detection device could enable precise measurements at record resolution, according to new research led by Adelaide University. An international team exploited an integrating sphere—a highly reflective hollow cavity that causes light to bounce around inside many times before exiting—to demonstrate a device that can measure the color (wavelength) composition of light with extreme precision at a resolution of just 6 femtometers.

science.title: Prison data analysis finds choosing lowest reoffending risk scores preserves overall accuracy
science.summary: Whether an individual reoffends after their release from prison or is successfully rehabilitated depends on several factors. When assessing the risk of recidivism, all of these are taken into account—both by human experts and by machine learning models. If several equally reliable computational models produce different risk ratings, the lowest value should be used for the individual concerned, suggest Ashwin Singh (TU Wien) and Carlos Castillo (ICREA/Universitat Pompeu Fabra).

science.title: Sexual violence can hide in plain sight at music festivals, according to new study
science.summary: The pressure to maintain an atmosphere of fun and escapism can make it harder for festival organizations to acknowledge and respond to harm, while frontline workers are left dealing with its consequences, a new study finds.

science.title: Swordfish may be using deep dives to navigate the open ocean
science.summary: Swordfish spend much of their time hunting prey about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface in the ocean twilight zone, but occasionally, they reach depths of more than 1,000 meters (3,280 feet). Now, scientists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) are investigating what may be behind these extreme dives.

science.title: AI-generated molecular fingerprints help identify existing compounds with therapeutic potential
science.summary: Health care researchers have long sought to harness the power of computing to design molecules that bind to specific receptors and can be used as targeted treatments for diseases. Even with the increasing sophistication of artificial intelligence, however, this technological promise has yet to be realized.

science.title: Detailed 3D view of babesiosis parasite's ribosome could guide development of targeted treatments
science.summary: A new study has revealed a three-dimensional, near-atomic-resolution view of the ribosome from Babesia divergens, one of several Babesia species known to infect humans and cause babesiosis. The structural insights from this close-up view could help researchers identify parasite-specific features that may be exploited for future drug development.

science.title: Germany's Isar Aerospace eyes overtaking Elon Musk's SpaceX
science.summary: The head of Germany's Isar Aerospace voiced hope Tuesday that the company could one day overtake Elon Musk's SpaceX to become the world's premier space launch company.

science.title: By carefully arranging molecules, scientists can control how a material responds to light, heat and physical force
science.summary: University of Missouri researchers have created a single solid material that responds differently depending on what it's exposed to. Shine light on it, and it changes from yellow to white, an indication of a chemical reaction. Heat it, and it undergoes a different chemical reaction. Scratch the surface, and it flashes blue.

Zenifar is a program associate at the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). environment.summary: The Daasanach people in the Turkana Basin of northern Kenya experienced the worst drought in 40 years between November 2020 and March 2023. The Daasanach are pastoralists who have lived semi-nomadically for roughly 6,000 years, supported by herds of livestock including cows, camels, donkeys, and goats. A group of researchers worked with the Daasanach to […]

environment.summary: ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Prominent climate change activist Greta Thunberg arrived Tuesday at the U.N. climate meeting, where she emphasized the need to protect people and the planet over profits and power. This year’s meeting — called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes after a year of climate-induced heat waves and other […]

environment.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
environment.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

environment.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
environment.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

environment.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
environment.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

mix_items.title: Mental health app may help unemployed people find jobs, six-week trial suggests
mix_items.summary: Losing a job can be a life-shattering experience. And when depression complicates a job search, unemployment can become a vicious cycle. Now, a Northwestern University–led clinical trial suggests a new intervention may break that cycle: a phone app, named DRIVEN, that combines weekly self-guided mental health exercises (to reduce stress and increase motivation) with job-seeking strategies.

mix_items.title: A new tool makes biodiversity conservation planning more efficient and reproducible
mix_items.summary: ZonationR is a new tool that simplifies the use of Zonation to identify priority areas for biodiversity conservation. It brings all stages of the conservation planning analysis together in one automated and reproducible workflow and helps users systematically explore and compare alternative conservation scenarios.

mix_items.title: How conversations shape decisions about dementia care
mix_items.summary: When someone is living with dementia, decisions about their care can have a significant impact on their health and quality of life. But how are these decisions made, particularly when family members or friends are also involved?

mix_items.title: Genetic ancestry plays a key role in the migration of Cory's shearwaters
mix_items.summary: To what extent do genes influence the migratory routes of birds? The factors that determine the long-distance migrations of seabirds are not yet fully understood. Now, a study published in the journal Molecular Ecology reveals that, in the case of Cory's shearwater, an individual's genetic ancestry is a more significant factor in their migratory decisions than their social environment in the breeding colony.

mix_items.title: Earliest known compact quasar pair poses a black hole growth puzzle
mix_items.summary: The oldest pair of compact quasars ever observed has been found only 900 million years after the Big Bang. Scientists say there is no theoretical explanation for how the pair of actively feeding black holes grew so massive at such an early time in the history of the universe. The pair of quasars has been given the Hawaiian nickname Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

mix_items.title: New organic iron-sulfur framework boosts photosynthesis and carbon fixation
mix_items.summary: Iron-sulfur clusters are ancient protein cofactors that are essential for electron transport, enzyme catalysis and photosynthesis. However, their sensitivity to oxygen and inherent instability have long hindered their practical application.

mix_items.title: How ripples in space-time can reveal new exoplanets
mix_items.summary: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets—worlds beyond our solar system—throughout our galaxy.

mix_items.title: European eels transmit a herpesvirus through bites, revealing another route for fish infections
mix_items.summary: Contrary to what was previously believed, viruses infecting fish are not transmitted exclusively through water acting as an abiotic vector. A team of researchers from the University of Liège has demonstrated that a virus affecting European eels can spread very efficiently through biting during aggressive interactions between individuals.

mix_items.title: Where AI can aid chemistry research and where reliability falls short
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Skoltech AI Center, together with colleagues from the Zelinsky Institute of Organic Chemistry of the Russian Academy of Sciences, ITMO University and other institutions, have published a paper in Chemical Society Reviews that examines where AI produces measurable value in a chemical research workflow, how to assess its reliability and why a strong benchmark result does not necessarily translate into laboratory performance.

mix_items.title: Cannabis addiction in pregnancy linked to higher risk of postpartum psychiatric crises
mix_items.summary: Women diagnosed with cannabis use disorder during pregnancy were more likely to end up in an emergency room for a psychiatric problem in the year after giving birth, according to a study of more than 2 million California deliveries.

mix_items.title: Repurposing the internet's backbone to advance whale monitoring
mix_items.summary: Bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut, at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics, has spent the past several years eavesdropping on the conversations of whales. But instead of using underwater microphones like other marine scientists, she listens by tapping into fiber-optic cables lying on the ocean floor—a powerful tool to aid in marine mammal conservation.

mix_items.title: Rerouting ships to avoid killing whale sharks has little cost, study finds
mix_items.summary: Redirecting shipping traffic to avoid collisions with whale sharks has very little impact on fuel use, according to new research led by the University of Southampton published in Royal Society Open Science.

mix_items.title: Ancient rocks reveal when Earth's tectonic engine 'switched on'
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified a major turning point in Earth's geological history, when the processes shaping the planet's crust changed dramatically and began to resemble the plate tectonics we see today—about 2.5 billion years ago.

mix_items.title: Going to the park at least once a week can improve children's mental health
mix_items.summary: Children who visit parks and playgrounds at least once a week may have better mental health and social development as they grow up. That's according to a new study by the University of Exeter, published in Epidemiology and Community Health. The paper is titled "Park Visits and Social-Emotional Development throughout Childhood: A Longitudinal Analysis of ALSPAC."

mix_items.title: High-achieving disadvantaged students are far less likely to take and pass entrance exams for selective schools
mix_items.summary: Disadvantaged students are less likely than their more advantaged peers with similar attainment to take and pass entrance exams for selective schools, and introducing an opt-out system for the tests would only deliver a small boost.

mix_items.title: Successful sleep apnea treatment may lead to unexpected weight gain
mix_items.summary: A new study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) and Soroka University Medical Center may have uncovered a biological mechanism behind why many adults and children gain weight following successful treatment for obstructive sleep apnea. The research, conducted on mice and published in Scientific Reports, suggests that the body retains a persistent "metabolic memory" that continues to drive increased appetite even after normal breathing is restored.

mix_items.title: Scientists anchor first scientific animal name to a modern-day spider
mix_items.summary: Scientists led by the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History have restored the physical reference of one of the most historically significant names in biology. In a paper published in Taxonomy, researchers designated a new type specimen, or neotype, for Araneus angulatus, the first animal species described using binomial nomenclature, the two-part naming system that scientists use today to identify and classify living organisms. The designation reconnects the name to a physical specimen decades after the original name-bearing spiders disappeared.

mix_items.title: Gamma radiation transforms brittle bioplastic into 'superstructure' hydrogel
mix_items.summary: Biomaterials engineers have created a "superstructure" hydrogel that could be an eco-friendly tool used in medical technologies and as a recovery aid for surgical procedures. The research is published in the journal Macromolecular Rapid Communications.

mix_items.title: Study identifies antidepressants that get patients well and keep them well
mix_items.summary: Worldwide, nearly 6% of people experience depression. Many of them continue taking antidepressants after achieving symptomatic improvement, among other reasons to prevent a relapse of depression. An international team of researchers investigated which antidepressants, if any, can not only get patients well but also keep them well (sustained response).

mix_items.title: Deaf patients get a raw deal in NHS hospitals, illustrative case history suggests
mix_items.summary: Deaf patients get a raw deal in NHS hospitals, suggests an illustrative case history of a deaf person's experience as an inpatient, published in the online journal BMJ Case Reports. During his hospital stay, reasonable adjustments to facilitate access to services—a key tenet of U.K. disability legislation—weren't made; the need for a professional British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter wasn't recognized soon enough; and frontline staff weren't adequately trained in how to support him.

mix_items.title: Government guidance indicates 95% of processed foods are unhealthy
mix_items.summary: More than 95% of processed or ultra-processed food products would be classified as unhealthy under UK government dietary guidance, according to new UCL-led research. The study, published in BMJ Medicine, found that the official public health definitions used to identify and regulate food and drink products in the U.K. varied widely in what proportion of processed and ultraprocessed products they classed as unhealthy, while systems such as traffic light labels failed to identify more than half of these unhealthy packaged foods.

mix_items.title: The psychology of saving electricity: How comparisons can curb consumption
mix_items.summary: Simple psychological interventions are often enough to encourage people to change their behavior—and this is also true when it comes to saving electricity. A new study by Mannheim-based consumer psychologist Dr. Yavor Paunov and colleagues shows that comparing one's own electricity consumption with that of others as well as practical energy-saving tips can help reduce energy consumption.

mix_items.title: Microscopy upgrade sharpens images fivefold without sacrificing tissue imaging depth
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Texas A&M University have cracked a problem that has limited biological imaging for years: seeing fine cellular detail while looking deep inside living tissue. The new microscopy technique resolves structures smaller than 100 nanometers, roughly a thousand times thinner than a human hair, without giving up the ability to image deep into intact samples.

mix_items.title: Three-layer model maps how protein-modifying enzymes may help regulate immunity
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Tsukuba have proposed a "three-tiered proteostasis model" for describing immune regulation by protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs), comprising protein arginine methylation, free methylarginine generation from protein turnover and methyltransferase-independent interactions with RNA and proteins. The framework integrates emerging evidence linking PRMTs to immune regulation, metabolism, vascular function and age-associated inflammation.

mix_items.title: Water molecules turn out to be secret messengers for magnetism
mix_items.summary: Water is not usually thought of as a magnetic material. But a new study led by researchers at Tohoku University's Institute of Multidisciplinary Research for Advanced Materials, in collaboration with National Taipei University of Technology (Taipei Tech), has found that tiny shifts in the orientation of water molecules can flip on magnetic partnerships between metal ions that are not even directly bonded to each other.

mix_items.title: Why does cancer rarely spread to the heart? Researchers develop organ-on-a-chip platform to find out
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of Toronto have created a new multi-organ-on-a-chip device to investigate why the heart is one of the least common sites of cancer metastasis, creating new opportunities for cancer research and drug discovery.

mix_items.title: Harnessing laser nuisance achieves record resolution for atomic measurements
mix_items.summary: A shoebox-sized color detection device could enable precise measurements at record resolution, according to new research led by Adelaide University. An international team exploited an integrating sphere—a highly reflective hollow cavity that causes light to bounce around inside many times before exiting—to demonstrate a device that can measure the color (wavelength) composition of light with extreme precision at a resolution of just 6 femtometers.

mix_items.title: Prison data analysis finds choosing lowest reoffending risk scores preserves overall accuracy
mix_items.summary: Whether an individual reoffends after their release from prison or is successfully rehabilitated depends on several factors. When assessing the risk of recidivism, all of these are taken into account—both by human experts and by machine learning models. If several equally reliable computational models produce different risk ratings, the lowest value should be used for the individual concerned, suggest Ashwin Singh (TU Wien) and Carlos Castillo (ICREA/Universitat Pompeu Fabra).

mix_items.title: Digitally supported care model improves serum urate target attainment in gout
mix_items.summary: For patients with gout, a physician-supervised treat-to-target (T2T) care model improves serum urate (SUA) target attainment, according to a study published online Nov. 4 in Arthritis & Rheumatology.

mix_items.title: Sexual violence can hide in plain sight at music festivals, according to new study
mix_items.summary: The pressure to maintain an atmosphere of fun and escapism can make it harder for festival organizations to acknowledge and respond to harm, while frontline workers are left dealing with its consequences, a new study finds.

mix_items.title: New biomarker may extend detection window for date-rape drug GHB
mix_items.summary: Every hour is critical when it comes to detecting the use of drugs used to render victims unconscious. The substance GHB, which is commonly used in this way, is excreted rapidly from blood and urine. Researchers at the University of Zurich have been evaluating a new biomarker using urine samples from real forensic cases. This biomarker can indicate earlier GHB intake even when the drug is no longer detectable using conventional analysis.

mix_items.title: Swordfish may be using deep dives to navigate the open ocean
mix_items.summary: Swordfish spend much of their time hunting prey about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface in the ocean twilight zone, but occasionally, they reach depths of more than 1,000 meters (3,280 feet). Now, scientists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) are investigating what may be behind these extreme dives.

mix_items.title: Lung ultrasound predicts progression of interstitial lung abnormalities in rheumatoid arthritis
mix_items.summary: Lung ultrasound (LUS) can predict radiologic progression of interstitial lung abnormalities (ILAs) in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), according to a study published in the November issue of Arthritis & Rheumatology.

mix_items.title: AI-generated molecular fingerprints help identify existing compounds with therapeutic potential
mix_items.summary: Health care researchers have long sought to harness the power of computing to design molecules that bind to specific receptors and can be used as targeted treatments for diseases. Even with the increasing sophistication of artificial intelligence, however, this technological promise has yet to be realized.

mix_items.title: About half have meaningful drop in long COVID symptoms by 36 months, study finds
mix_items.summary: About one-half of persons with likely long COVID (LC) after first severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection experience a meaningful reduction in symptoms by 36 months, according to a study published online Nov. 3 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

mix_items.title: Detailed 3D view of babesiosis parasite's ribosome could guide development of targeted treatments
mix_items.summary: A new study has revealed a three-dimensional, near-atomic-resolution view of the ribosome from Babesia divergens, one of several Babesia species known to infect humans and cause babesiosis. The structural insights from this close-up view could help researchers identify parasite-specific features that may be exploited for future drug development.

mix_items.title: Prostate cancer drug combination adds toxicity without clear benefit for tumors lacking targetable mutations
mix_items.summary: The prospective, multicenter, randomized phase 2 ZZ-FIRST clinical trial, led by the Vall d'Hebron Institute of Oncology's (VHIO) Prostate Cancer Group, evaluated the androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) enzalutamide plus the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) talazoparib versus enzalutamide alone in patients with high-tumor-burden metastatic prostate cancer who had not previously received hormone therapy.

mix_items.title: Germany's Isar Aerospace eyes overtaking Elon Musk's SpaceX
mix_items.summary: The head of Germany's Isar Aerospace voiced hope Tuesday that the company could one day overtake Elon Musk's SpaceX to become the world's premier space launch company.

mix_items.title: By carefully arranging molecules, scientists can control how a material responds to light, heat and physical force
mix_items.summary: University of Missouri researchers have created a single solid material that responds differently depending on what it's exposed to. Shine light on it, and it changes from yellow to white, an indication of a chemical reaction. Heat it, and it undergoes a different chemical reaction. Scratch the surface, and it flashes blue.

mix_items.summary: “Last night we had a very big fight with an elephant in our tomato field,” said Joeman Moyo, a farmer at Den Staat farm in South Africa’s Limpopo region. “We used a torch … to make a fire. The elephant would go away but return when I put out the torch. I also burned a […]

mix_items.summary: Kenya’s fitness boom runs on activewear built for stretch, sweat and shine yet almost no one asks what’s actually in the fabric. By 7 a.m. on a Saturday, Riverside Square in Nairobi’s Westlands neighborhood is already filling up. mix_items.summary: A recent Mongabay investigation by Elizabeth Claire Alberts and Andrés Alegría reveals that the Clarion-Clipperton Zone of the Pacific Ocean, a swath of deep sea regulated by the International Seabed Authority, has received a surge of claim applications filed with the United States for mineral exploration and exploitation. While the ISA, a U.N.-associated body, is […]

mix_items.title: ‘You need strong willpower’: IUCN’s Kazi Zenifar Azmiri on being a woman wildlife biologist
mix_items.summary: For more than a decade, Kazi Zenifar Azmiri has played a crucial part in protecting wildlife in Bangladesh. Zenifar is a program associate at the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Her work centers primarily on the rescue and rehabilitation of threatened vultures like the white-rumped vulture (Gyps bengalensis) and Himalayan griffon vulture (Gyps […]

mix_items.title: Drought reshapes livelihoods of Kenya’s Daasanach pastoralists, study finds
mix_items.summary: The Daasanach people in the Turkana Basin of northern Kenya experienced the worst drought in 40 years between November 2020 and March 2023. The Daasanach are pastoralists who have lived semi-nomadically for roughly 6,000 years, supported by herds of livestock including cows, camels, donkeys, and goats. A group of researchers worked with the Daasanach to […]

mix_items.title: Greta Thunberg arrives at UN climate talks saying ‘everything we love is at stake’
mix_items.summary: ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Prominent climate change activist Greta Thunberg arrived Tuesday at the U.N. climate meeting, where she emphasized the need to protect people and the planet over profits and power. This year’s meeting — called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes after a year of climate-induced heat waves and other […]

mix_items.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
mix_items.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

mix_items.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
mix_items.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
mix_items.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

satire_ro.title: Sute de pesediști își verifică amantele, să se asigure că nu sunt spioane
